AnomalyAug · Sep 2026

A certification flight that failed, and the test rig it produced

Design · build · flight test · anomaly investigation

A Level 1 high-power certification vehicle built from a fiberglass kit, with a switch-band avionics bay I designed and printed. The bay carries the altimeter, the arming switch, and both ejection charge canisters in a 5 in coupler sitting flush with the airframe. Because a certification flight is the first flight of the configuration, I flew single deploy (one channel, one charge, main at 600 ft) to keep the number of untested things as low as possible.

Decisions and what they cost

Printed AV bay
Self-designed switch band over a purchased coupler. Bought geometry and iteration speed; paid in material properties I did not yet understand.
Single deploy
Traded recovery redundancy for fewer untested elements. A dual-deploy failure at apogee is unrecoverable. That reasoning held. The altimeter's did not.
Epoxy sequence
Internal fin fillets before the aft centering ring: the most structural joint in the fin can cannot be reached afterward. 30-minute epoxy throughout.
Stability
2.13 calibers simulated, inside the 1.5–2.5 band. Verified against measured CG rather than the kit's published mass.

Anomaly report · late main deployment

Observed
Main deployed at roughly 100 ft AGL against a commanded 600 ft. About 500 ft of descent was unarrested.
Damage
Printed coupler fractured cleanly along a single layer plane. Upper airframe separated with the avionics bay attached.
Consequence
Certification not achieved. The EasyMini was not recovered, so the dataset that would answer root cause is gone, the more expensive of the two failures.
  1. H1 · check firstConfiguration error. The deploy altitude actually written to the EasyMini may not be the one I meant to write. Cheapest to rule out, so it goes first regardless of likelihood.
  2. H2 · leadingStatic port response lag. A barometric altimeter reads bay pressure, not ambient. Layer-line porosity acts as an undersized, unpredictable port; on a fast main-only descent the bay lags, the altimeter reads high, and the main fires late. Late, not absent, exactly what happened.
  3. H3 · secondaryStructural. Five perimeters is right for in-plane loading and wrong for this load. FDM parts are anisotropic and the crack never had to cross a wall. Print orientation put the weak plane normal to deployment shock.
Test method
Vacuum rig built to measure lag, not accuracy. Static accuracy at a held vacuum looks fine and tells you nothing. The rig pulls vacuum, holds, then releases quickly while logging EasyMini output against a reference pressure sensor. The gap between the two curves during the release is the bay's time constant.

Corrective action for the reflight

Load path
Deployment load carried by two 1/4-20 threaded rods bulkhead to bulkhead, not by the printed coupler wall.
Material & orientation
Switch band reprinted in PETG, oriented so layer lines run perpendicular to the ejection load.
Data
Second logging altimeter and a tracker added. Nothing flies again with a single point of failure on the data.
Verification
Ground test of charge sizing before flight day; altimeter config read back and photographed on the pad.

Reflight · September 4, 2026

The reflight flew on September 4, reconfigured to dual deploy. The corrective actions held: the avionics bay came through clean, the vehicle was recovered whole, and for the first time the flight was fully logged: the dataset the first attempt never produced. The drogue fired exactly at apogee. The main did not.

The first failure was structural and cost me the data. The second cost me the certification and nothing else, because this time the bay survived to tell me what happened.

Anomaly report · main did not deploy

Observed
Drogue deployed nominally at apogee. At the main event the charge fired, but the parachute never left the airframe: the ejection gas drove it forward into the hollow nose cone and pressurized it there instead of separating it. Descent under drogue only; hard landing, vehicle intact.
Recovered
Everything. Redesigned bay held, altimeter logged the full flight, airframe survived the drogue-speed landing. The first attempt's structural and data-loss failures are closed.
Consequence
Certification not achieved. But this is a visible failure: the data is complete, and it is a mode I had flagged as a risk before the flight rather than a surprise.
  1. H1 · leadingNose cone dead volume vented the charge. The main packs against a hollow nose cone with no bulkhead closing off its cavity. Ejection gas took the path of least resistance into that dead volume, compacting the chute forward rather than shearing the pins and pushing the pack out.
  2. H2 · secondaryCharge undersized for the true volume. Sizing that would separate a closed coupler can be too small once the gas can expand into the nose cavity. Pressure on the separation plane never reached shear-pin break force.
  3. H3 · checkPack friction. Chute and shock cord packed tight enough that static friction, plus the vented volume, exceeded the charge's usable work before separation.
Design direction
Close off the dead volume and make the gas act on the separation plane: a nose bulkhead or shoulder plug so pressure works on the coupler joint instead of venting forward, a deployment bag or piston so the charge pushes a hard surface rather than compacting fabric, and ground-tested charge sizing for the as-packed configuration. The RockSim file for this flight is being finalized and will be overlaid on the trace above once it lands.

Learning the whole vehicle before leading the next one

Flight preparation · systems knowledge · team leadership

During the 2025–2026 season, I shadowed Stony Brook's Battle of the Rockets team lead as the intended successor. I joined after the initial build work, then helped test and prepare the vehicle for competition. By launch weekend, I could assemble and disassemble the entire rocket and understood how its airframe, avionics, recovery system, and Mars rover payload fit together.

The team launched in Culpeper, Virginia, on April 10–11, 2026. The rocket reached 1,459 ft, and both the vehicle and Mars rover worked as intended. I became team lead in August 2026 and now lead our NASA Student Launch effort. Our proposal has been submitted, and we are awaiting NASA's selection decision.

Shadowing gave me more than a handoff document. I learned the complete vehicle, watched where the previous process added unnecessary work, and carried those lessons into the way I now plan tests and train the next team.

Battle of the Rockets flight

Simulation 80
OpenRocket projected 1,871.89 ft on a J525LW, within the required flight window of at least 1,000 ft and below 4,000 ft.
Measured flight
Maximum height 1,459 ft, maximum speed 245 ft/s (Mach 0.2), and maximum boost acceleration 136 ft/s² (4.22 G).
Timing
3.1 s boost, 6.3 s coast, 120.3 s descent, and 129.7 s total flight time.
Recovery and payload
Main descent rate was 12 ft/s. The rocket and Mars rover completed their intended functions.

Lessons carried into the next season

Preserve Blue Tube
The previous vehicle's Blue Tube was sanded without a functional reason. That removed part of the material's weather and humidity resistance, so surface preparation now has to follow the actual bonding or finishing requirement.
Design for access
The avionics bay used twist-and-tape arming. It worked, but made assembly and disassembly difficult. A dedicated switch band provides a cleaner, more repeatable interface for testing and flight preparation.
Build dual-deploy knowledge
No one on the previous team had implemented dual deployment. I am learning it directly through my L1 vehicle so the current team can approach drogue-at-apogee and main deployment with tested procedures instead of assumptions.
Learn the complete system
By competition, I could assemble and disassemble the full rocket. That system-level understanding now helps me connect subsystem decisions and train members beyond a single assigned component.

How confined bubbles become foam

Experiment design · imaging · data analysis

Air injected into a vertical 2 mm square channel filled with glycerol, water, and surfactant. At that scale a bubble large enough to touch the walls stops being round and becomes a capsule, and how those capsules pack and drain decides whether the column stays a bubble train or turns into foam. The governing question: how do gas and liquid flow rates, with liquid composition, control bubble morphology, spacing, drainage, and the transition to confined foam?

Early runs showed behavior the existing variables could not explain. I proposed adding viscosity as a controlled variable, which turned a drainage measurement into a composition study.

Flow-regime classification

IBO      O         OIndependent bubbles. Discrete, clear liquid separation, no persistent grouping.
CBOO    OOO      O     OOClustered. Individually recognizable, but generation and spacing are heterogeneous.
BO O O O O O OConsecutive bubbles. Little long liquid separation, structures still visibly round.
S()()()()()()Consecutive ovals. Elongated capsules one after another under strong confinement.
X────────Gas-dominated. Liquid pushed out of the observation region; train structure lost.

Distinctions the data depends on

Ql = 0 is not still liquid
It means no imposed injection. Liquid already in the column keeps draining under gravity. Injection and drainage get separate symbols.
Morphology is not drainage
A flow can show independent bubbles and drain hard at the same time. The regime map and the drainage map are plotted separately.
d/h is not d/L
d/h is aspect ratio: shape. d/L is size relative to spacing: packing. Conflating them destroys the packing result.
Irregular is not bad data
Variable timing at low flow may be the defining signature of the clustered regime, so we compute the coefficient of variation of inter-bubble period, not just a mean.

RX faultSince 2026

Printed airframe, full electronics bring-up

Structures · integration · tuning · debug

A 5-inch quadcopter built from the frame up. Topology-optimized Fusion 360 frame printed in PETG; SpeedyBee F405 V3 stacked with a 50 A 4-in-1 ESC, running Betaflight with DSHOT600 and hand-tuned PID loops. Topology optimization is only as good as the load case you feed it, and a simulated thrust load is a guess about a vibration environment I have not characterized. Flying first means the next frame revision comes from accelerometer data and observed failure locations.

Frame FEA is sequenced behind electronics bring-up on purpose. I want measured loads off a flying airframe, not assumed ones.

Open fault

Symptom
Receiver link established and worked, then stopped, with no configuration or hardware change in between.
Under investigation
Bind state lost on the receiver; a UART or protocol mismatch that only surfaces after a firmware or power cycle; an intermittent solder joint on the RX pad. Working the list cheapest-first.
